newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cenbank sees no room for monetary changes.
newsitem.headline: Czech cenbank sees no room for monetary changes.

text.p: The Czech National Bank governing board said on Thursday that the current economic situation, despite massive flooding and the need for flood relief funds, left no room for a change in monetary policy.
"The current situation does not create any room for a change in the orientation of the monetary policy," the CNB's spokesman Martin Svehla said in a statement following a regular board meeting.
It said that the possibility to further ease interest rates was conditional on "lowering the existing imbalances in the external (trade) relations and... public budgets".

The central bank board said that government plans to provide relief for areas in the east of the country which have been devastated by flooding since last week should not mean a retreat from austerity measures taken to relieve recent macroeconomic pressures.

"Under given circumstances it is suitable to consider also an exceptional short-term personal income tax increase. This method would be healthiest for national economic policy and would contribute toward the stability of the currency," the statement said.
The central bank has been gradually lowering interbank interest rates since hiking them to prohibitive levels amid speculative attacks on the Czech crown in late May.

The central bank was forced to float the currency. That was followed by government spending cuts to lower domestic demand which has ballooned the current account deficit to more than eight percent of GDP and put the crown under pressure.
The board said it was necessary this year to keep public budgets -- state and local -- in balance.

The government last week approved bond issues of up to five billion crowns and made available another six billion crowns in state assets in order to fund relief efforts in the flooded areas where damage is estimated to total 50 to 100 billion crowns.

The finance ministry said on Thursday that the government would consider a loan offer from the European Investment Bank which might exceed 10 billion crowns for infrastructure reconstruction projects.
